{{Short description|Are certain algebras finitely generated}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Hilbert's fourteenth problem''', the fourteenth of [[Hilbert's problems]] proposed in 1900, asks whether certain [[algebra]]s are [[finitely generated]].

Let <math>k</math> be a [[field (mathematics)|field]] and let <math>K</math> be a subfield of the [[field of rational functions]]
:<math>k(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math>
containing <math>k</math>. Hilbert asked whether the <math>k</math>-algebra
:<math>R: =K\cap k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]</math>
is always finitely generated over <math>k</math>.<ref name="Hilbert1902">{{cite journal |last=Hilbert |first=David |author-link=David Hilbert |title=Mathematical problems |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=8 |issue=10 |pages=437–479 |year=1902 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1902-00923-3|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The answer is negative in general, but depends strongly on dimension. Writing <math>r=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K</math> for the [[transcendence degree]] of <math>K</math> over <math>k</math>, {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Oscar Zariski|first= Oscar|last=Zariski|year=1954}} proved that <math>R</math> is finitely generated whenever <math>r\leq 2</math>; in particular, the answer is affirmative for <math>n\leq 2</math>.<ref name="Zariski1954">{{cite journal |last=Zariski |first=Oscar |author-link=Oscar Zariski |title=Interprétations algébro-géométriques du quatorzième problème de Hilbert |journal=Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques |volume=78 |pages=155–168 |year=1954|ref=none}}</ref> [[Masayoshi Nagata]]  constructed the first counterexamples in 1958, one of which he announced at the 1958 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]]; his first construction has <math>n=32</math> and <math>r=4</math>.<ref name="Nagata1960">{{cite conference |last=Nagata |first=Masayoshi |author-link=Masayoshi Nagata |title=On the fourteenth problem of Hilbert |book-title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Edinburgh, 1958 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=459–462 |year=1960 |mr=0116056 |ref=none}}</ref><ref name="Freudenburg2001">{{cite journal |last=Freudenburg |first=Gene |title=A survey of counterexamples to Hilbert's Fourteenth Problem |url=https://www.math.bas.bg/serdica/2001/2001-171-192.pdf|journal=Serdica Mathematical Journal |volume=27 |pages=171–192 |year=2001}}</ref>

In characteristic zero, Shigeru Kuroda subsequently constructed counterexamples with <math>n=4</math> and <math>r=3</math> in 2004, and with <math>n=3</math> in 2005.<ref name="Kuroda2004">{{cite journal |last=Kuroda |first=Shigeru |title=A counterexample to the Fourteenth Problem of Hilbert in dimension four |journal=Journal of Algebra |volume=279 |issue=1 |pages=126–134 |year=2004 |doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2004.05.002|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Kuroda2005">{{cite journal |last=Kuroda |first=Shigeru |title=A counterexample to the fourteenth problem of Hilbert in dimension three |journal=Michigan Mathematical Journal |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=123–132 |year=2005 |doi=10.1307/mmj/1114021089|doi-access=free}}</ref> Thus the bounds are sharp: finite generation always holds when <math>n\leq2</math> or <math>r\leq2</math>, whereas counterexamples already occur with <math>n=r=3</math>.

== History ==

The problem originally arose in algebraic [[invariant theory]]. Here the ring <math>R</math> is given as a (suitably defined) ring of polynomial invariants of a [[linear algebraic group]] over a field <math>k</math> acting algebraically on a [[polynomial ring]] <math>k[x_1, ..., x_n]</math> (or more generally, on a finitely generated algebra defined over a field).

In this situation the field <math>K</math> is the field of rational functions (quotients of polynomials) in the variables <math>x_i</math> which are invariant under the given action of the algebraic group, and the ring <math>R</math> is the ring of polynomials which are invariant under the action.

A classical example in the nineteenth century was the extensive study (in particular by [[Arthur Cayley|Cayley]], [[James Joseph Sylvester|Sylvester]], [[Alfred Clebsch|Clebsch]], [[Paul Gordan]] and also Hilbert) of invariants of [[binary form]]s in two variables under the natural action of the [[special linear group]] <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(k)</math>.

Hilbert proved finite-generation results for invariant rings arising from important classical group actions in characteristic zero. These results were subsequently extended, notably by [[Hermann Weyl]], and in modern form invariant rings of [[reductive group|reductive algebraic groups]] acting on finitely generated algebras are finitely generated. By contrast, invariant rings of non-reductive groups need not be finitely generated; Nagata's counterexample is a suitably constructed ring of invariants for a linear action of a non-reductive [[linear algebraic group]].

A major ingredient in Hilbert's proof is the [[Hilbert basis theorem]] applied to the [[ideal]] inside the polynomial ring generated by the invariants.

== Zariski's formulation ==

[[Oscar Zariski|Zariski]] gave an algebro-geometric formulation of Hilbert's fourteenth problem in terms of [[quasi-affine variety|quasi-affine varieties]]. More precisely, the rings of global [[regular function]]s on irreducible normal quasi-affine varieties are, up to isomorphism, precisely the rings of the form <math>L\cap A</math>, where <math>A</math> is a normal finitely generated <math>k</math>-domain and <math>L</math> is a subfield of its field of fractions containing <math>k</math>.<ref name="Winkelmann2003">{{Citation | last = Winkelmann | first = Jörg | title = Invariant rings and quasiaffine quotients | journal = Math. Z. | volume = 244 | issue = 1 | pages = 163&ndash;174 | year = 2003 | doi = 10.1007/s00209-002-0484-9 | postscript = .| arxiv = math/0007076 }}</ref> Thus Hilbert's question can equivalently be viewed as asking whether the ring of global regular functions on such a quasi-affine variety must be finitely generated.

{{harvtxt|Zariski|1954}} proved that <math>L\cap A</math> is finitely generated when <math>\operatorname{trdeg}_k L\leq 2</math>. In particular, Hilbert's original problem has an affirmative answer for <math>n\leq 2</math>. See also [[Zariski's finiteness theorem]].

== Nagata's counterexample ==

[[Masayoshi Nagata|Nagata]] constructed the first counterexamples to Hilbert's fourteenth problem in 1958.<ref name="Nagata1959">{{citation| last = Nagata| first = Masayoshi| year = 1959| title = On the 14-th Problem of Hilbert| journal = American Journal of Mathematics | volume = 81 | issue = 3 | pages = 766–772 | doi = 10.2307/2372927
}}</ref> The following example was announced at the 1958 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]].

Let <math>\pi</math> be the prime field of a field <math>k</math> and let
:<math>k=\pi(a_{ij}\mid 1\leq i\leq 3,\ 1\leq j\leq16),</math>
where the 48 elements <math>a_{ij}</math> are algebraically independent over <math>\pi</math>. Let
:<math>A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_{16},t_1,\ldots,t_{16}]</math>
be the polynomial ring in 32 variables. Let <math>V</math> be the 13-dimensional subspace of <math>k^{16}</math> consisting of the vectors <math>(b_1,\ldots,b_{16})</math> orthogonal to each of
:<math>(a_{i1},\ldots,a_{i16}),\qquad i=1,2,3.</math>

With its additive group structure, <math>V</math> is isomorphic as an algebraic group to <math>\mathbb G_a^{13}</math>. An element <math>(b_1,\ldots,b_{16})\in V</math> acts on <math>A</math> by
:<math>t_j\mapsto t_j,\qquad x_j\mapsto x_j+b_jt_j\qquad (1\leq j\leq16).</math>
Nagata proved that the invariant ring <math>A^V</math> is not finitely generated over <math>k</math>. If <math>L</math> is the field of invariant rational functions, then <math>A^V=L\cap A</math>, so this gives a counterexample to Hilbert's original formulation. For this example, <math>n=32</math> and <math>r=19</math>.

Nagata's other counterexample, published in his 1959 paper, also has <math>n=32</math>, but has <math>r=4</math>.<ref name="Nagata1959" />

== Later counterexamples ==

Further counterexamples were constructed with progressively fewer variables. {{harvtxt|Roberts|1990}} gave a counterexample with <math>n=7</math> and <math>r=6</math>. It was later realized as the invariant ring of a nonlinear action of the additive group <math>\mathbb G_a</math>.<ref>{{citation | last = Deveney | first = James K.| last2 = Finston| first2 = David R. | year = 1994 | title = {{math|G<sub>a</sub>}}-actions on {{math|C<sup>3</sup>}} and {{math|C<sup>7</sup>}} | journal = Communications in Algebra | volume = 22 | issue = 15 | pages = 6295–6302|doi=10.1080/00927879408825190}}</ref>
Related constructions gave counterexamples with <math>(n,r)=(6,5)</math> by Gene Freudenburg<ref>{{citation | last = Freudenburg | first = Gene | year = 2000 | title = A counterexample to Hilbert's Fourteenth Problem in dimension six | journal = Transformation Groups | volume = 5 | issue = 1 | pages = 61–71 | doi = 10.1007/BF01237178 }}</ref> and with <math>(n,r)=(5,4)</math> by Daniel Daigle and Freudenburg.<ref>{{citation
| last = Daigle| first = Daniel | last2 = Freudenburg
 | first2 = Gene | year = 1999 | title = A counterexample to Hilbert's Fourteenth Problem in dimension 5 | journal = Journal of Algebra | volume = 221
 | issue = 2 | pages = 528–535 | doi = 10.1006/jabr.1999.7987|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The subsequent counterexamples of Kuroda reached the theoretical lower bounds for both <math>r</math> and <math>n</math>. In 2004, Shigeru Kuroda constructed counterexamples with <math>(n,r)=(4,3)</math>, showing that the lower bound on <math>r</math> is sharp.<ref name="Kuroda2004"/> In 2005, he constructed a counterexample with <math>(n,r)=(3,3)</math>.<ref name="Kuroda2005"/> This also attains the smallest possible value of <math>n</math>, since Zariski's theorem gives an affirmative answer for <math>n\leq2</math>.

In the linear invariant-theoretic setting, {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Shigeru Mukai|first=Shigeru|last=Mukai|year=2004}} constructed, over the complex numbers, linear actions of the three-dimensional additive group <math>\mathbb G_a^3</math> whose invariant rings are not finitely generated. {{harvtxt|Totaro|2008}} extended such counterexamples to arbitrary fields, giving in particular a linear action of <math>\mathbb G_a^3</math> on <math>\mathbb A^{18}</math> with a non-finitely generated invariant ring.
